extracted.intended_audience: Department of Defense hospital administrators, military health analysts, and policymakers responsible for workload/accounting/ resource allocation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for measuring hospital output and productivity in military medical facilities, comparing the Composite Work Unit and the proposed Health Care Unit (HCU), including formulations, performance factors, weighting methods, peer grouping, and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of changes in average length of stay on Composite Work Unit
rubrics_metrics.description: The Composite Work Unit measurement does not have a built-in factor to account for changes in length of stay; decreased inpatient lengths of stay can reduce occupied bed days and thus decrease perceived productivity even when actual productivity or care intensity increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study adjusted occupied bed days to 1979 length of stay, computed Composite Work Units for both years, and adjusted by the American Hospital Association's 'Hospital Intensity Index' to demonstrate that after adjustment productivity actually increased. Warning: without such adjustments, policy successes (shorter stays) may appear as declines in productivity because CWU treats every occupied bed day the same. Quote: Composite Work Unit 'makes no distinction between a 'necessary' occupied bed day and an 'unnecessary' occupied bed day.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption that all occupied bed days are equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: The Composite Work Unit assumes all occupied bed days are equivalent despite differing patient needs by illness, severity, age, sex, and complications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This causes measured productivity to fall when extra effort shortens hospital stays. Authorities note early days of stay require far more staff utilization; therefore measures that count bed days equally misrepresent actual workload. Recommendation: account for differing care intensity rather than treating bed days as uniform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to differentiate types of manhours in CWU
rubrics_metrics.description: CWU does not differentiate between different types of manhours; it aggregates physician, nurse, and ancillary personnel hours as equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/critique: 'Time is not a pure factor and one hour of physician time has considerably greater relative value than a similar amount expended by an orderly.' Different mixes of staff can produce the same outpatient visit but with different resource implications; CWU will measure same workload irrespective of differing professional mixes or cost of time.

rubrics_metrics.name: No distinction between 'easy' and 'hard' cases
rubrics_metrics.description: CWU does not distinguish between easy cases (require little hospital resources) and hard cases (require extensive resources).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: hospitals providing extensive, complex services may appear less productive compared with those providing routine non-complex care. This affects inter-hospital comparisons unless case mix complexity is accounted for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadequate accounting for technological advances and changing product mix
rubrics_metrics.description: The Composite Work Unit was developed before many modern services (e.g., dialysis, organ transplants, complex radiology, inhalation therapy) and does not adequately account for such procedures in its computations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Result: rapidly evolving technologies and more complex service mixes are undercounted in CWU. Recommendation: measurement systems must update service categories/weights to reflect new technologies and procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: CWU unsuitable as a long-term funding allocator without price adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: Using CWU as a general resource allocator assumes the cost to produce one CWU remains constant over time; this is false given large increases in medical care costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A study concluded the base unit should be adjusted to reflect absolute changes in prices of factors involved in meeting workload requirements (example: cost for same quantity of care increased ~80% between FY1957 and FY1971). If used for funding, update base units to reflect price inflation and changing input costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-service comparability problems due to differing output measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons among Navy, Army, and Air Force are difficult because Navy and Army use Composite Work Unit outputs while Air Force uses Adjusted Admission Equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not a criticism of CWU per se but of inconsistent methods across services; two different output-element measurement methods may preclude valid inter-service comparisons unless standardized or converted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health Care Unit design characteristics (desired properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Designers specified that the Health Care Unit (HCU) should: (1) be expressed as a single number; (2) not be adjusted for facility type; (3) make minimal use of proxies; (4) use existing data bases; (5) be adaptable and flexible to allow future changes; (6) not measure quality of care but quantity of care provided; and (7) be useful at all levels throughout the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These seven characteristics guided HCU formulation and serve as design criteria when evaluating or constructing a hospital output measure. Tradeoffs (e.g., not adjusting for facility type vs. need to account for case mix) should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: General HCU approach (partition, count treatments, weight, aggregate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach: partition total types of care into homogeneous categories (performance factors), determine number of 'treatments produced', take a weighted sum to smooth differences in treatment requirements, and compute a single number indicating hospital output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This methodological framework emphasizes using homogeneous categories and weights based on resource consumption to produce a comparable aggregate output measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Uniform Chart of Accounts (UCA) Performance Factors as HCU inputs
rubrics_metrics.description: The designers decided the Uniform Chart of Accounts provides needed performance factors; HCU inputs are the 25 Performance Factors (six inpatient dispositions, six inpatient occupied bed day accounts, eleven ambulatory care visits, and two dental accounts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhibit VII lists all 25 Performance Factors (e.g., Inpatient Medical Dispositions, Medical OBD, Ambulatory Medical CV, Dental Services WDP). Use these standardized summary accounts as the basis for P_i in HCU computation to leverage existing reporting (Medical Expense and Performance Report).

rubrics_metrics.name: HCU mathematical formulation (HCU = Σ P_i * W_i)
rubrics_metrics.description: HCU is computed as HCU = Σ (P_i * W_i) where P_i is the ith performance factor and W_i is the weight factor computed from the cost of providing corresponding health services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose of W_i: determine relative value of one performance factor versus another (i.e., resource intensity). HCU can be interpreted as 'that amount of care which has the value of one dollar' because weights are based on monetary resources required to produce the service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for weight development using internal UCA cost data (four variants)
rubrics_metrics.description: When using internal cost data from the Medical Expense and Performance Report, designers considered four methods to develop weights: (1) overall average cost per service (DOD-wide total cost divided by sum of performance factors); (2) mean by hospital (average cost per performance factor at each hospital, then mean these means); (3) mean by hospital adjusted for extremes (same as 2 but discard outliers beyond a specified SD); (4) median by hospital (take the middle hospital's average cost for the performance factor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each yields a candidate W_i; resulting weights would be multiplied by P_i totals to calculate output indices. Choice among these methods affects sensitivity to outliers and representativeness; designers discussed discarding extreme values to stabilize weights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of external civilian data for weight computation — pros and cons
rubrics_metrics.description: External data from civilian hospitals or CHAMPUS were considered for weights, but civilian billing practices (physician billing separate from hospitals) and geographic cost variation make national/regional/local choices problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems: civilian costs not uniform geographically; civilian physician fees vary locally while military salaries are standardized. Using national civilian costs may misweight facilities in different areas. If external data used, decide national/regional/local aggregation carefully and account for billing differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling duplicate inpatient performance information (dispositions vs. occupied bed days)
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance factors include both inpatient dispositions and occupied bed days which duplicate information for the same patient; designers considered: (1) use dispositions only (set OBD weights to 0), (2) use occupied bed days only (set disposition weights to 0), (3) direct regression on output using both measures (weighted sum), or (4) indirect regression — convex linear combinations of methods (1) and (2) — and select best explanatory number for expense variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice affects how inpatient resource use and length of stay are captured. Designers later recommended regression-based approaches to allocate credit between disposition and bed day accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency and method of updating weights
rubrics_metrics.description: Designers debated updating weights continuously, quarterly, annually, by base year, cumulative, or by exponential smoothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final recommendation: do not update continuously; recompute weights at 3- to 5-year intervals to provide stability for interpretation and comparability, while still reflecting significant changes in medical services output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outpatient weight computation and outlier treatment (designer recommendation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended outpatient weight computation: for each hospital compute outpatient UCA cost for the performance factor divided by the sum of corresponding performance factors (i.e., cost per performance factor). Combine these numbers across hospitals, compute mean and standard deviation, discard numbers deviating by more than two standard deviations, recompute mean, then divide each by the fiscal year average cost per disposition to obtain final normalized weights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedure normalizes outpatient visit weights relative to inpatient disposition cost (example: divide $21.21 outpatient cost by $1,129.89 FY avg cost per disposition to get modified weight .019). Outlier removal (>|2 SD|) stabilizes weights across hospitals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inpatient weight computation via length-of-stay regression
rubrics_metrics.description: For inpatient weights compute each hospital's average length of stay for the account (occupied bed days / dispositions) and cost per disposition; plot pairs (length of stay, cost per disposition) for hospitals and perform least squares regression. The intercept (vertical axis) gives the disposition weight and the slope gives the occupied bed day weight, both divided by the fiscal year average cost per disposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method partitions fixed (admission-day) and variable (additional bed days) costs between disposition and bed-day performance factors and yields normalized weights scaled to FY average cost per disposition. Exhibit IX/X illustrate the process and resulting original/modified weights.

rubrics_metrics.name: HCU normalization and interpretability (unit meaning and uses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Weights are normalized so HCU can be interpreted as resource-based units (e.g., 'that amount of care which has the value of one dollar'), allowing HCU to be used similarly to CWU to calculate productivity indices (HCU per physician, per employee, per employee manhours, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because weights are based on cost, HCU indicates intensity of care and can be aggregated across facilities or expressed per input to measure productivity. Ensure normalization is consistent when comparing over time or across groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer grouping refinement to account for case mix and facility differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation to place hospitals into peer groupings (Categories I, II, III) because hospitals vary in nature and complexity of cases; grouping criteria include HCU accumulated, Full Time Equivalents (FTE), number of physicians, and operating beds (e.g., Category I: 0–9,000 HCU, <500 FTE, <30 physicians, <70 beds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute weights within peer groups to reflect facility type/case mix. Peer grouping reduces bias from aggregating dissimilar hospitals and helps produce single measures appropriate to each facility category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-group weight computation using fixed and variable cost partitioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Within peer-group methodology, treat admission day costs as fixed charges and 2nd+ bed days as variable charges; compute fixed ($/disp) and variable ($/bed day) costs for each inpatient account and normalize by FY average cost per disposition to obtain weights for disposition and occupied bed day accounts (example: Wx = 329.30/990.44 = .332 and Wy = 113.6/990.44 = .114).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This indirect regression and fixed/variable partition allocate 'credit' for care across performance factors for a given inpatient stay, eliminating need to zero out certain performance factors and addressing case-mix differences by peer group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and objections to HCU (Navy non-concurrence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite refinements, HCU still includes occupied bed days and thus assumes hospitalization is required for a given illness; differences in treatment modalities and admission rates across services (e.g., Navy admission rates much lower) can bias HCU outputs and resource allocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: If HCU used as input for resource allocation, services with lower admission-based 'credit' (more outpatient treatment) could be disadvantaged or pressured to change treatment modalities to gain resources. Consider potential perverse incentives and validate cross-service comparability before using HCU for funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation on stability vs. responsiveness of weights
rubrics_metrics.description: Designers recommended balancing stability for interpretability with update frequency to maintain accuracy: recompute weights at 3–5 year intervals to reflect present level of medical services output while providing comparability over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This repeats guidance on update frequency but emphasizes the tradeoff: frequent updates increase responsiveness to change but reduce comparability; multi-year intervals were chosen as compromise.
